period: Swenett, Greek Syene: Egypt's frontier town from about 3000 BC to today
summary: Egypt began here: the frontier town at the First Cataract, where Nubian gold and ivory came in, and a Greek used the noon sun to measure the Earth.
look: Stand on the Corniche on the east bank and face west. The river, about 650 metres wide just upstream, is broken by granite islands: the long one in front is Elephantine, the ancient town, with Kitchener's Island and its gardens behind it. On the west bank a cliff riddled with tomb doorways rises under a small domed shrine, and further south, on a hill, stands the pink mausoleum of the Aga Khan. Upstream to the south, out of sight, lie the old dam, the High Dam and Philae.
story:
The Egyptians called this town Swenett; the Greeks called it Syene. Egyptians oriented themselves facing south, towards the source of the Nile, so for them the country did not end here, it began here. Just upstream lay the First Cataract, a maze of boulders and rapids that made a natural border. Under every dynasty Swenett was a garrison town, and every boat passing north or south paid tolls. Through it came the riches of Nubia: gold, ebony, incense and ivory. The island opposite was called Abu, 'elephant'.

The hills here gave Egypt its finest hard stone. Red granite from Aswan went into obelisks, colossal statues, shrines and sarcophagi the length of the country, and an abandoned obelisk still lies in its quarry on the edge of town.

Around 240 BC Eratosthenes, the scholar who ran the Library of Alexandria, used a report about Syene: at noon on midsummer's day the sun stood almost straight overhead, shining down a deep well. Comparing that with the shadow cast at Alexandria on the same day, and the distance between the two cities, he calculated the circumference of the Earth. (Strictly, Syene is not exactly on the tropic: on the solstice a staff still cast a tiny shadow, about one four-hundredth of its length.)

By 1900 Aswan was a winter resort for Europeans, and since the dams it has also been the heart of Egyptian Nubia. Your two days here hold a felucca on the river, the Botanical Garden, Philae, the Nubian Museum, the Unfinished Obelisk and the souq. The pace is slower than Cairo's. Enjoy it.
details: From the Corniche: the long island opposite is Elephantine; its rounded grey boulders may be what gave it the name 'elephant'.
On the west-bank cliff, the small dome on the summit: Qubbet el-Hawa, the Dome of the Wind, above the Tombs of the Nobles.
On the hill further south-west, the pink Fatimid-style mausoleum of the Aga Khan.
In the souq: heaps of dried red hibiscus flowers, Aswan's signature crop, sold for karkade.
At the south end of the Corniche, on its granite rock, the terracotta-coloured Old Cataract Hotel.
fun_fact: Geologists' word 'syenite' comes from Syene, the Greek name for Aswan; the irony is that Aswan's famous stone is, technically, a granite.
narration:
You are standing at the southern gate of ancient Egypt. In front of you the Nile is wide and scattered with granite islands, and just upstream, to your left, lay the First Cataract, a barrier of boulders and rapids.

The Egyptians called this town Swenett, and the Greeks called it Syene. Egyptians faced south, towards the source of the Nile, so for them the country did not end here. It began here. Every passing boat paid customs. Through this gate came the riches of Nubia: gold, ebony, incense and ivory. The long island in front of you is Elephantine, and its Egyptian name simply meant elephant.

Aswan also gave Egypt its finest hard stone. Red granite from these hills went into obelisks, colossal statues and royal sarcophagi all down the Nile.

Now a Greek story. Around 240 BC Eratosthenes, the scholar who ran the Library of Alexandria, heard that at noon on midsummer's day the sun at Syene shone almost straight down a well. In Alexandria, at that moment, a stick still cast a shadow. From that angle and the distance between the two cities, he worked out the size of the whole Earth.

Over the next two days you will sail a felucca, visit Isis at Philae, and meet Nubia in its museum. Before you go, look across to the far bank: the small dome on top of the cliff marks the Tombs of the Nobles.

period: A living tradition; the cataract tamed by the dams of 1902 and 1970
summary: A wooden boat with one huge sail and no engine, on the rocky stretch of river that marked Egypt's southern border for most of its history.
look: A felucca is an open wooden boat under one big triangular lateen sail, hung from a long sloping yard; it usually takes about ten passengers with a crew of two or three. Sit low and keep your head clear when the captain swings the yard. A typical loop goes round Elephantine and Kitchener's Island, along the west bank under the Tombs of the Nobles and the Aga Khan's hill, and back past the Old Cataract Hotel. The dark, rounded boulders all around are the visible edge of the old cataract zone.
story:
The felucca works with the two forces that shaped Egyptian life. The current flows north; the prevailing wind blows from the north. So for thousands of years boats drifted downstream with the mast lowered and sailed upstream under canvas. When your captain swings the yard across and the boat zigzags, he is tacking, climbing into the wind one diagonal at a time.

The First Cataract was not a waterfall. The word comes from Greek for 'flowing down', but this was a stretch of shallow water broken by granite boulders and rocky islets. For most of Egyptian history it was the southern frontier: cargo between Egypt and Nubia was unloaded and reloaded at Syene and Philae. Since the first Aswan dam of 1902 the old cataract has been drowned under the water behind it.

Myth gathered here. The Egyptians believed the flood rose from caverns beneath the cataract, guarded by the ram god Khnum. Herodotus was told in Egypt that the springs of the Nile lay between two hills near Syene and Elephantine and were bottomless; he suspected his informant was joking. On Sehel Island, upstream, expedition leaders cut hundreds of inscriptions into the rocks, including the Famine Stela, a Ptolemaic text claiming that King Djoser ended seven years of famine by honouring Khnum.

Agree the price, the route and the time before you board; the price is usually per boat per hour. With no wind it will be slow, and that is part of the charm. A small tip for the boy who sings or helps with the sail is welcome.
details: Watch the captain tack: he swings the long yard across the mast and the boat zigzags into the wind.
On the west bank, rows of doorways cut in the cliff: the Tombs of the Nobles under the Dome of the Wind.
The smooth grey-black boulders around Elephantine, polished by the river; some really do look like bathing elephants.
On the hill to the south-west, the Aga Khan's pink mausoleum; below it, his white villa by the water.
Sehel Island and its inscriptions lie further upstream; short rides rarely reach it, so ask if you want to go.
fun_fact: In hieroglyphs, 'to travel south' is written with a boat under full sail and 'to travel north' with a boat whose mast is down: the wind blows upriver, the current flows down.
narration:
You are on a felucca, a wooden Nile boat with one great triangular sail on a long sloping yard. There is no engine, so listen: water on the hull, the creak of rope, maybe a captain humming.

This boat works with two forces the ancient Egyptians built their world around. The current flows north, and the wind mostly blows from the north. So for thousands of years boats drifted downstream with the mast down and sailed upstream with the sail up. In hieroglyphs, the word for travelling south is a boat under sail, and travelling north is a boat with no sail at all. When your captain swings the yard across and the boat zigzags, he is tacking, climbing into the wind one diagonal at a time.

Just upstream lay the First Cataract. Not a waterfall, but a maze of granite boulders and rapids. For most of history it was Egypt's southern border, and cargo had to be unloaded and carried around it. The Egyptians believed the flood itself rose from caverns beneath these rocks, guarded by the ram god Khnum. The Greek historian Herodotus was told that the Nile's springs lay here, bottomless, between two hills, and he suspected his informant was joking.

Since the first dam in 1902 the rapids have been tamed. Look now at the boulders around you: smooth, dark and rounded, like elephants bathing.

period: British era, early 20th century; a government research garden since
summary: A whole island turned into a garden by Lord Kitchener: royal palms, trees from India and busy birds, in the middle of the Nile.
look: The island is about 750 metres long and less than half a kilometre wide; feluccas land at the south-eastern end. A main avenue runs up its spine under tall royal palms, with side paths through beds and groves. Walk the length and have your boat collect you at the far end.
story:
The island is named after Horatio Herbert Kitchener, the British general who reconquered Sudan in 1898 and later governed Egypt as Britain's Consul-General from 1911 to 1914. Accounts differ on when the island came to him; Wikipedia ties the gift to his consul years. What is clear is what he did with it. With help from the Ministry of Irrigation he turned 750 metres of Nile island into a garden of exotic trees, many brought from India, laid out with walkways for strolling.

After Kitchener the island passed to the Egyptian government and became a research station, the Botanical Research Institute. The collection he began has been tended ever since: royal palms with smooth grey trunks, sabal palms, and subtropical trees from Asia and Africa.

Today it is where Aswan families come for weekend picnics and where hot travellers come for shade. The birds are part of the show: hoopoes probing the lawns, and tiny iridescent sunbirds working the flowering shrubs.
details: The royal palm avenue along the island's spine: smooth grey trunks so regular they look poured from concrete.
On the lawns, early or late in the day: hoopoes, cinnamon-coloured with a punk crest and a long curved bill.
In flowering shrubs: tiny metallic sunbirds sipping nectar like hummingbirds.
Any tree hung with long, heavy, sausage-shaped fruit is an African sausage tree; do not linger under it in a breeze.
From the island's west edge, look across at the golden dunes of the desert bank.
fun_fact: Kitchener's face became the most famous recruiting poster in British history in 1914, yet his gentlest legacy is this garden of palms.
narration:
This whole island is a garden, and it began as one man's project. It is known as Kitchener's Island, after Lord Kitchener, the British general who took Sudan in 1898 and later governed Egypt as Britain's Consul General. With help from the Ministry of Irrigation he turned 750 metres of Nile island into a park of exotic trees, many brought from India, with shaded walks for strolling.

Later it became a government research station, and his collection has been tended ever since. Look up at the royal palms along the main avenue: smooth grey trunks so regular they look poured from concrete.

Today Aswan families come here for weekend picnics, and so do the birds. Walk the full length of the island and ask your boat to pick you up at the far end. On the way, watch the lawns for hoopoes, cinnamon-coloured birds with a punk crest and a long curved bill, and the flowering shrubs for tiny sunbirds flashing green and purple.

period: Border fortress from about 3000 BC; town into the Roman period
summary: Ivory Island: Egypt's border fortress for 3,000 years, with temple ruins, a Nilometer, a Jewish garrison's papyri and Nubian villages.
look: Elephantine is about 1.6 km long and 450 m wide at its widest. The southern end, around the Aswan Museum, is the ruin field of ancient Abu: mounds of mud-brick houses, the temples of Khnum and Satet, and the Nilometer stairs down to the river. The middle of the island holds Nubian villages with painted houses; a hotel tower stands at the northern end.
story:
The Egyptians called the island Abu, 'elephant', perhaps because ivory was traded here, perhaps because the rounded grey boulders on its banks look like elephants bathing. The Greeks translated the name as Elephantine. A fort stood here by about 3000 BC, under the First Dynasty, and for most of Egyptian history this was the frontier: customs post, garrison, and the base from which caravan leaders like Harkhuf set out south. Its governors were buried in the cliff opposite, at Qubbet el-Hawa.

Its temples served the gods of the cataract: Khnum the ram, Satet, protector of the border, and Anuket of the rapids. Satet's shrine began around 3000 BC as a niche between boulders and was rebuilt on the same spot for some 3,000 years.

Since 1969 the German Archaeological Institute, with Swiss colleagues, has taken the town apart layer by layer. Finds range from a mummified sacred ram of Khnum, now in the island's museum, to the Aramaic papyri of a 5th-century BC Jewish garrison. Temples of Thutmose III and Amenhotep III stood nearly intact until 1822, when they were demolished during Muhammad Ali's campaign to conquer Sudan.
details: South of the museum: low mud-brick walls of houses from many centuries, stacked like a layer cake.
The partly rebuilt temple of Satet, over the spot where her cult began between boulders.
At the southern tip: the platform and gateway of the Khnum temple.
Near the museum, the Nilometer stairs running down to the water.
In the villages: doorways and walls painted in blue, ochre and white.
fun_fact: Elephantine has produced documents in hieratic, demotic, Aramaic, Greek, Latin and Coptic: a postbag from one border town spanning many centuries.
narration:
This island was Egypt's southern frontier post for about 3,000 years. Its ancient name was Abu, which means elephant. Maybe because ivory changed hands here, maybe because of the smooth grey boulders on its banks that look like elephants bathing. The Greeks translated the name: Elephantine.

A fort stood here by about 3000 BC. Boats paid customs, soldiers watched the south, and caravan leaders set off from here into Africa.

The town honoured the gods of the cataract: Khnum the ram, who released the flood, Satet, guardian of the border, and Anuket of the rapids. Satet's first shrine was a niche between boulders around 3000 BC, and her temple was rebuilt on the same spot again and again for 3,000 years.

Since 1969 German and Swiss archaeologists have been peeling this mound apart, layer by layer. That is what the low brick walls around you are: houses stacked on houses. Look for the rebuilt temple of Satet, then walk down towards the river to find the Nilometer stairs.

period: Site used from the Old Kingdom; temple rebuilt in Dynasty 30 and the Ptolemaic period
summary: The house of Khnum, the potter who shaped people and released the flood, next to the shrine of a local governor who became a saint.
look: At the southern tip of Elephantine the Khnum temple survives mostly as a raised platform, column bases and a granite gateway. Among the town ruins nearby are the walled sanctuary of Heqaib and the partly rebuilt temple of Satet.
story:
Khnum, the ram-headed god of the cataract, was said to control the Nile flood from caves beneath this island and to shape every child on his potter's wheel. His temple here is recorded as early as the Third Dynasty and was rebuilt from scratch in the 30th Dynasty, just before Alexander's conquest; little stands today beyond the platform and gateway.

More personal is the sanctuary of Heqaib, a Sixth Dynasty governor of Elephantine who was worshipped after his death as a local saint. In the Middle Kingdom, later governors such as Sarenput I added shrines and statues beside his, so the little sanctuary kept growing for generations.
details: The raised platform of the Khnum temple at the island's southern tip, with its granite gateway.
The Satet temple, partly rebuilt by the excavators, near the boulders where her cult began.
The Heqaib sanctuary: a walled court lined with shrines added by Middle Kingdom governors.
From the tip of the island, look across the water to the Old Cataract Hotel.
fun_fact: Heqaib is a rare case of an ordinary official becoming a god: centuries after his death, governors still queued to place their statues next to his.
narration:
These ruins at the island's southern tip were the house of Khnum, the ram-headed god of the cataract. Egyptians said he kept the Nile flood in caverns under this island and let it out each summer. He was also a potter, shaping every child on his wheel before birth. His temple here goes back at least to the Third Dynasty, and it was rebuilt from scratch in the 30th Dynasty, just before Alexander the Great arrived.

Nearby is a more personal shrine. Heqaib was a local governor of the Sixth Dynasty, and after his death people worshipped him as a saint. Later governors set up their own statues beside his. Look for the walled court of his sanctuary among the ruins of the town.

period: Pharaonic origins; last rebuilt in Roman times; used into the 19th century
summary: A staircase into the Nile that doubled as a tax calculator: the higher the flood climbed these steps, the more Egypt paid.
look: Elephantine has two Nilometers. The famous one is a stone corridor with a staircase descending to the river, associated with the temple of Satet; its walls carry scales in Arabic, Roman and hieroglyphic numerals. The second, probably older, is a rectangular basin at the island's southern tip near the Khnum temple, opposite the Old Cataract Hotel.
story:
Between July and November the Nile used to spill over its banks and spread black silt over the fields. Too little flood meant famine; too much washed villages away. A Nilometer told the authorities exactly where the year stood, and because Elephantine was Egypt's southern border, this was the first place the rising water could be measured.

The reading was also a tax bill. A good flood meant a good harvest, so the state expected more. Access was restricted to priests and officials: a reading was power. The Greek geographer Strabo described a Nilometer here, though nobody can be sure which of the two he meant. After the Arab conquest, the general Amr ibn al-As reported to the caliph that 16 cubits gave an abundant harvest and 18 brought disaster.

The corridor Nilometer was last rebuilt in Roman times and was still in use in the 19th century; deep marks cut at the water's edge go back to the 17th Dynasty. Since the High Dam was completed in 1970 the river no longer floods at all.
details: Walk down the corridor stairs and read the wall scales: Arabic, Roman and older numerals side by side.
At the bottom, by the water, older marks cut deep into the rock.
The square basin near the Khnum temple at the island's tip: the second, probably older, Nilometer.
From the stairs, look across the water to the Old Cataract Hotel on the east bank.
fun_fact: In Cairo, the right to read the Roda Nilometer was handed to a scholar in 861 and stayed with his descendants for more than three centuries.
narration:
You are at the Nilometer of Elephantine, a staircase running down into the Nile like a ruler laid on its side. Before the dams, the river flooded every summer, spreading black silt over the fields. Too low a flood meant hunger. Too high, and villages washed away. Priests came down these steps to read exactly how high the water stood.

Elephantine was the southern border, so the rising flood could be measured here first.

The reading was also a tax bill. A high flood meant a rich harvest, so the state demanded more. After the Arab conquest, the general Amr ibn al As told the caliph that 16 cubits gave an abundant harvest, and 18 meant disaster. The Greek geographer Strabo described a Nilometer here, though no one knows which of the island's two he meant.

This corridor was last rebuilt in Roman times and still used in the 19th century. Since the High Dam was finished in 1970, the river no longer floods. Look at the walls now: you can find scales in Arabic, Roman and older numerals side by side.

period: Founded 1912; finds from prehistory to the Roman period
summary: A quiet villa museum on Elephantine full of the island's own finds, starring a mummified sacred ram of Khnum.
look: The museum stands at the southern end of Elephantine beside the ruins of ancient Abu. The old building is a villa in a garden; a newer annexe just to the north, added in the early 1990s, shows what the German excavations found on the island: pottery, tools, weapons, statues and mummies.
story:
The British Egyptologist Cecil Firth set up the museum in 1912, at first to hold finds from Nubia gathered as the old dam's reservoir rose. The villa is often said to have been built for Sir William Willcocks, the engineer of the first Aswan dam.

Since 1969 the German Archaeological Institute has excavated the island, and the annexe displays its finds: everyday objects from the frontier town, Middle Kingdom statues of officials, and mummies of the ram, the sacred animal of Khnum. It is usually quiet, cool and unhurried.
details: The mummified ram: the living animal of Khnum, embalmed and buried with honour on the island.
Statues of Middle Kingdom officials; several came from the sanctuary of the deified governor Heqaib.
In the annexe: pots, tools and weapons from the town, arranged by period.
The garden between the buildings, and the path down to the Nilometer.
fun_fact: Rams were mummified on Elephantine because each was a living image of Khnum; this museum is one of the few places you can meet one face to face.
narration:
This small museum on Elephantine tells the island's own story. It was set up in 1912 by the British Egyptologist Cecil Firth, in a villa often said to have been built for Sir William Willcocks, the engineer of the first Aswan dam. The newer annexe nearby shows what German archaeologists have found on the island since 1969: pottery, tools, weapons and statues from 3,000 years of frontier life.

The star is a mummified ram. Rams were the living animal of Khnum, the god of the cataract, and his sacred rams were embalmed and buried here with honour. Find the ram first, then look for the Middle Kingdom officials in stone, with their calm, watchful faces.

summary: A Jewish garrison's letters and contracts from 2,400 years ago: marriages, divorces, a festival letter, and a temple burned by its neighbours.
look: There is little to see on the ground. The Aramaic papyri came from houses at the northern edge of the town mound, an 'Aramaic quarter' found in 1907, and the originals are scattered across museums in Berlin, Brooklyn, Cairo, London, Munich and Paris. Stand among the town ruins and picture the neighbourhood where they were written.
story:
In the 5th century BC Egypt was part of the Persian empire, and Elephantine's garrison included Judean soldiers and their families. They wrote in Aramaic, the empire's office language, and the dry soil kept their papers: loans, house sales, marriage and divorce contracts, the freeing of slaves. The archive of a woman named Mibtahiah follows her property and marriages across decades.

The community had its own temple to Yahweh, which stood near the temple of Khnum. In 410 BC it was destroyed, the documents say at the instigation of Khnum's priests, and letters survive asking the Persian governor Bagoas for help to rebuild it. A letter of 419 BC gives instructions for the Festival of Unleavened Bread.
details: The northern edge of the ruin mound: the Aramaic papyri came from houses on this side.
Look south towards the Khnum temple: the two temples were close neighbours.
One theory for the conflict: Khnum was a ram god, and the Passover sacrifice of lambs may have offended his priests.
The largest collection of Elephantine documents is in Berlin, not here.
fun_fact: Belzoni and Drovetti were buying papyri from this archive in the 1810s, but nobody realised they came from Elephantine until almost a century later.
narration:
Somewhere in these town ruins, about 2,400 years ago, Jewish soldiers and their families lived and wrote letters. In the 5th century BC Egypt was part of the Persian empire, and this border fort had a Judean garrison. They wrote in Aramaic, and the dry soil kept their papyri: loans, house sales, marriage and divorce contracts. One woman, Mibtahiah, left a whole family archive.

They even had their own temple to Yahweh, close to the temple of the ram god Khnum. In 410 BC it was destroyed, the letters say at the urging of Khnum's priests, and the community wrote to the Persian governor for help. Look south towards the Khnum temple: the neighbours were that close.

period: Late Period to Roman, about 380 BC to AD 300; closed about AD 537
summary: The island of Isis: the last place the old gods were worshipped, and a temple moved stone by stone to save it from the Nile.
look: Boats land at the southern tip of Agilkia island by the Kiosk of Nectanebo, the oldest building. From there a long forecourt between two colonnades leads north to the first pylon; behind it are the birth house, the second pylon, the hypostyle hall and the sanctuary of Isis. Trajan's Kiosk stands on the east shore near the small temple of Hathor, and the Gate of Hadrian on the west side of the main temple. Allow at least two hours.
story:
The original island of Philae was small, about 380 metres by 120, just above the cataract. Its oldest certain temple, a kiosk of Psamtik II in the 6th century BC, gives the first evidence of Isis worship here. Nectanebo I added a temple around 370 BC, but more than two-thirds of what survives was built by the Ptolemies, the Macedonian Greek kings of Egypt, and Roman emperors kept adding to it up to Caracalla.

Isis was the wife of Osiris and the mother of Horus, the great magician who brought her murdered husband back to life. Philae became her greatest sanctuary, overtaking Elephantine. Pilgrims came from Egypt and Nubia and, in Ptolemaic times, from Anatolia, Crete and mainland Greece, and many scratched their names into the walls. Next door, the island of Bigeh was believed to hold the tomb of Osiris.

Philae outlived the old religion elsewhere. Nubian peoples kept worshipping here under treaty, and the last known hieroglyphic inscription (AD 394) and the last demotic one (452) were carved on this island. According to Procopius, Justinian had the temple closed in 537.

In modern times the island was nearly lost. The first Aswan dam (1902) left it flooded for much of the year, and the High Dam threatened it permanently. Between 1977 and 1980 the whole complex was dismantled and rebuilt here on Agilkia, reshaped to match Philae's outline. A Greek footnote: an obelisk from Philae, carried to England by William Bankes, helped Champollion decipher hieroglyphs, because it repeated Cleopatra's name in Greek and Egyptian.
details: From the landing, look north up the forecourt to the twin towers of the first pylon.
Greek and Latin graffiti left by ancient pilgrims, scratched on many walls and doorways.
Coptic crosses cut over pagan reliefs: the temple's second life as a church.
On the east shore, Trajan's Kiosk: the island's ancient front door from the river.
From the west side, look across to Bigeh island, the sacred tomb of Osiris.
fun_fact: In 2014 the European Space Agency named its comet lander Philae, after the obelisk that helped crack hieroglyphs; its target landing site was called Agilkia.
narration:
Welcome to Philae, the island of Isis. Strictly speaking, this is not Philae at all. The island under your feet is Agilkia, and every temple on it was moved here, block by block, in the 1970s, from an island about 500 metres away that now lies under the water.

The goddess here is Isis: wife of Osiris, mother of Horus, the great magician who brought her murdered husband back to life. A shrine to her stood on Philae by the 6th century BC, but almost everything you see was built later. First came Nectanebo the First, of the last native dynasty, then the Ptolemies, the Macedonian Greek kings of Egypt, and finally Roman emperors adding the finishing touches.

Pilgrims came from all over Egypt, from Nubia in the south, and even from Crete and mainland Greece, and many scratched their names into the walls. Nubians kept coming long after Rome turned Christian. That is why Philae holds the very last hieroglyphic inscription ever carved, in AD 394. The emperor Justinian finally had the temple closed around AD 537.

Your route: the long colonnaded forecourt, the great first pylon, the birth house, the hypostyle and the dark sanctuary of Isis, then out to Hadrian's Gate and Trajan's Kiosk by the water. Start by looking north up the forecourt to the twin towers of the first pylon.

period: Kiosk: Nectanebo I, 380-362 BC; colonnades Ptolemaic and Roman
summary: Where every visitor lands: the oldest building on the island, Hathor faces on the columns, and a forecourt where no two capitals match.
look: At the southern landing stands the Kiosk of Nectanebo I, a small hall of columns with Hathor-faced capitals, linked by screen walls. North of it the forecourt opens between two colonnades: the long west one, with windows that once looked out onto the river, and the shorter east one, left unfinished. Off the east side is the small temple of Arensnuphis. At the far end rises the first pylon.
story:
The kiosk is the oldest thing standing on Philae. Nectanebo I, founder of the 30th Dynasty, the last native Egyptian line, built it around 370 BC as the vestibule of an earlier temple of Isis. When the Ptolemies built the great temple further north, the kiosk stayed at the island's southern tip as the porch where pilgrims came up from the river. Its capitals carry the cow-eared face of Hathor.

The Ptolemies and Romans then laid out the long forecourt, which narrows towards the pylon because it follows the shape of the old island. The west colonnade is the showpiece: walk it and compare the capitals, palm, papyrus and lotus combined differently each time. Its windows once opened straight onto the Nile. The east colonnade was never finished, and some capitals are still roughed-out blocks.

The small temple of Arensnuphis, a Nubian god, received additions from the Nubian king Arqamani in the late 3rd century BC, a sign of how close Philae stood to Nubia. Not long after, Ptolemy V had Arqamani's cartouches erased.
details: On the kiosk columns: Hathor's face with cow ears, beneath a little shrine-shaped top.
West colonnade: walk slowly and compare the capitals; palm, papyrus and lotus never repeat the same way.
The west windows: on old Philae the Nile lapped right below them.
East colonnade: unfinished capitals, still blocky, show the stages of carving.
The small Arensnuphis temple off the east side: a Nubian god in an Egyptian temple.
fun_fact: The Nubian king Arqamani built here in the late 200s BC; a few years later Ptolemy V had his name chiselled out of the walls.
narration:
You have just landed where pilgrims always landed, at the southern tip of the island. The little pavilion of columns is the oldest building on Philae. Nectanebo the First, founder of the last native Egyptian dynasty, built it around 370 BC as the porch of an earlier temple of Isis. Look at the column tops: the face of Hathor, goddess of music and joy, with her cow ears.

Now turn north. The long forecourt in front of you was laid out by the Ptolemies and the Romans, and it narrows towards the great pylon because it follows the shape of the old island. Walk up the colonnade on your left, the west side, and compare the capitals. Palm fronds, papyrus and lotus, combined differently every time. Its windows once opened straight onto the Nile.

The colonnade on the right was never finished: some capitals are still rough blocks. Near it stands a small temple to Arensnuphis, a Nubian god, which a Nubian king helped to build. Find one roughed-out capital on the east side, then compare it with a finished one on the west.

period: Ptolemaic; pylon reliefs of Ptolemy XII, 80-51 BC
summary: Cleopatra's father smiting enemies before Isis, Napoleon's soldiers signing in, and the house where the goddess gave birth to Horus.
look: The first pylon is two towers about 18 metres high with a gateway between them, guarded by two granite lions. On the front, the king grasps a bunch of enemies by the hair and raises his club before Isis, Horus and Hathor. Inside the gateway passage is a French inscription of 1799. Through the gate, the mammisi (birth house) runs along the left, west side of the court, its columns topped with Hathor faces.
story:
A pylon was the horizon in stone: two mountains with the sun rising between them, the gateway into the god's house. The smiting king on this one is Ptolemy XII Neos Dionysos, nicknamed Auletes, 'the flute-player', father of Cleopatra VII. In life he was driven out by his own Alexandrians and restored with Roman help; on the wall he crushes the world. Temple reliefs were not news, they were eternity. An older gateway of Nectanebo I is built into the pylon, and in front of it stood a pair of obelisks; one was carried off to England by William Bankes in the 19th century.

The pylon is also a visitors' book. Greek inscriptions on the towers are cut through by later Egyptian figures. Three Romans left their names here in the summer of 116 BC, the oldest known Latin inscriptions in Egypt. Inside the gateway a French text records that in 1799 General Desaix's division of Napoleon's army pursued the Mamluks beyond the cataracts.

The mammisi celebrated the birth of Horus. Isis hid in the papyrus marshes to bear and nurse her son, safe from his murderous uncle Seth. Because every king was Horus, the reliefs cast the king as the divine child: the Macedonian Ptolemies presenting themselves as true sons of Isis. The Nubian king Arqamani also contributed to the building.
details: On the pylon front: the giant smiting king, Ptolemy XII, before Isis, Horus and Hathor.
The two granite lions at the foot of the gateway.
Inside the main gateway: the neat French inscription left by Napoleon's expedition in 1799.
In the court, on the left: the mammisi, with Hathor-faced capitals on its columns.
On the mammisi walls, look for Isis with the infant Horus among papyrus.
fun_fact: Ptolemy XII's Greek nickname, Auletes, means the flute-player: the conqueror on this pylon was remembered in Alexandria for his music.
narration:
In front of you is the first pylon of the temple of Isis: two massive towers, about 18 metres high, with the gate between them. To an Egyptian, a pylon was the horizon, two hills with the sun rising between them.

Look at the big figures on the front. The king grabs a cluster of enemies by the hair and raises his club, while Isis, Horus and Hathor look on. That king is Ptolemy the Twelfth, Cleopatra's father, nicknamed Auletes, the flute player. In real life his own people in Alexandria drove him out, and Rome had to put him back on the throne. On this wall he conquers the world. Temple walls were not news, they were eternity.

Walk into the gateway and look for a neat inscription in French. It records that in 1799 the division of General Desaix, of Napoleon's army, chased the Mamluks beyond the cataracts. Visitors have been signing this temple for over 2,000 years, including three Romans in 116 BC, the oldest Latin writing known in Egypt.

Through the gate, on your left, is the mammisi, the birth house. Here Isis gives birth to Horus, hidden in the papyrus marshes from his murderous uncle Seth. And who appears as the divine baby? The king himself. A Greek dynasty was telling Egyptians: we are the children of Isis. Look on its walls for the goddess with her infant among the papyrus.

period: Ptolemaic, 3rd-2nd century BC; a church from the 6th century AD
summary: Colour still on the columns, Coptic crosses cut over the gods, and the dark room where Isis lived for some 800 years.
look: The second pylon stands at the north end of the court; at its base a natural granite outcrop was left in place and smoothed into a stela of Ptolemy VI. Through it, the hypostyle hall has ten columns with painted floral capitals, crosses carved on the walls and a Christian altar. Beyond are three small vestibules and, at the back, the windowless sanctuary with a granite pedestal for the sacred boat of Isis. Stairs lead to the Osiris chapels on the roof, usually closed.
story:
The builders of the second pylon met a lump of bedrock granite and, instead of removing it, dressed it into a stela recording a grant of land by Ptolemy VI. Behind the pylon the hypostyle hall is the temple's roofed forest: each step inward was darker, lower and holier. Its capitals keep much of their green, blue and red.

After the temple was closed in the 6th century, this hall became a church of St Stephen, and inscriptions credit Bishop Theodore with the conversion. Christians carved crosses into the walls and chiselled away the faces of the old gods, though figures of Horus are often oddly spared.

The sanctuary is small and windowless. Here the statue of Isis stood in its shrine. Every morning a priest broke the seal on the shrine, woke the goddess, washed, dressed and fed her, then sealed her in again. The granite pedestal in the middle carried her portable barque, the boat in which she travelled in procession; it is usually attributed to Ptolemy III and Queen Berenice.

On the roof, if open, small chapels show the death and resurrection of Osiris: his body laid out, and Isis restoring him to life.
details: At the base of the second pylon: the natural granite outcrop smoothed into a stela of Ptolemy VI.
Hypostyle capitals: look up for original green, blue and red paint.
Coptic crosses cut into the walls and doorways, and gods with hacked-out faces.
In the sanctuary: the granite pedestal that carried the barque of Isis.
The stair to the roof and the Osiris chapels, if the guards have it open.
fun_fact: Christians defacing the reliefs often left Horus untouched; one suggestion is that the falcon-headed son of a divine mother seemed too close to their own story.
narration:
You are passing from the court into the heart of the temple. Before you go in, look down at the base of the second pylon. The builders hit a lump of natural granite and, instead of removing it, they smoothed it into a stela, recording a gift of land by King Ptolemy the Sixth.

Inside is the hypostyle hall, a roofed forest of columns. Look up. The capitals, flowers and palm leaves still carry their green, blue and red after more than 2,000 years. The dimness is deliberate: each step deeper into an Egyptian temple is darker, lower and holier.

Now look for crosses. In the 6th century, after the temple closed, Bishop Theodore turned this hall into a church of Saint Stephen. Christians carved crosses into the walls and chiselled away the faces of the old gods, though Horus is often oddly spared. A Christian altar survives from those days.

Go through the three small rooms beyond and you reach the sanctuary. It is tiny, with no windows. Here stood the statue of Isis in her shrine. Every morning a priest broke the seal, woke the goddess, washed, dressed and fed her, then sealed her in again. The granite pedestal in the middle once carried her sacred boat for processions. Stand still in the dark for a moment, and look at that pedestal.
